When working within the Java Collections Framework, ArrayList is the ubiquitous contiguous-memory data structure developers rely on for fast random access by index. Unlike arrays with fixed allocations, an ArrayList provides the illusion of infinite dynamic scaling. To understand how ArrayList grows dynamically, one must look directly beneath its high-level API into its internal implementation. Under the hood, an ArrayList wraps a standard, raw Java object array designated as transient Object[] elementData. When elements are continuously appended past the bounds of this current array buffer, the list must orchestrate a resizing lifecycle.

The mechanics of this scaling behavior are governed entirely by the default capacity and the growth factor. When you instantiate a parameterless ArrayList using its default constructor, the initial backing array is not immediately allocated with a large size; instead, it is lazily initialized to a shareable empty array instance (DEFAULTCAPACITY_EMPTY_ELEMENTDATA). Upon the insertion of the very first element via add(), the capacity is inflated to the default capacity of 10. Subsequent insertions that exceed this threshold trigger the growth factor calculation. Historically and standardly in the OpenJDK implementation, the growth factor increases the existing capacity by 50 percent, computed via bitwise operations as oldCapacity + (oldCapacity >> 1). This ensures that memory consumption scales amortized O(1) for appending operations while preventing excessive, premature memory exhaustion.

rows: First add() on empty default instance

items: When an add operation detects that elementData.length is equal to the current size, it invokes the private grow(int minCapacity) method.
The growth algorithm first calculates a preferred new capacity by taking 1.5 times the current capacity using the bit shift operator (oldCapacity + (oldCapacity >> 1)).
If this new capacity is still insufficient to satisfy the requested minCapacity, the algorithm adopts minCapacity as the baseline target.
The engine then checks against Integer.MAX_VALUE - 8 (accounting for VM-specific array header overheads) to prevent OutOfMemoryError crashes caused by array size limitations.

Finally, Arrays.copyOf() is executed behind the scenes, allocating a completely new contiguous block of memory in the heap and copying all existing object references over before discarding the old array for garbage collection.

parsed_answer.content: Senior Production Gotcha: Relying on the default growth factor of 1.5x for massive datasets introduces severe performance bottlenecks and memory fragmentation. Every time an ArrayList crosses its threshold (e.g., from 10 to 15, 22, 33, 49...), the JVM must allocate a brand-new contiguous memory block on the heap, copy all existing references via System.arraycopy, and leave the old array subject to garbage collection pressure. If you are instantiating lists that will hold hundreds of thousands of items, always pass an explicit initial capacity to the constructor to completely bypass intermediate array allocations and allocations churn.

title: How does ArrayList grow dynamically? What is the default capacity and growth factor?
